newsitem.title: USA: B.A.T barred int'l issues from settlement-state AG.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T barred int'l issues from settlement-state AG.

text.p: B.A.T Industries Plc led the cigarette industry's opposition to addressing the issue of marketing to teenagers outside the United States when negotiating a tobacco settlement this spring, a U.S. attorney general said on Tuesday.
"We were not able to do that... B.A.T is the reason we were not," Christine Gregoire, the Washington state attorney general, told the Senate Commerce Committee.
She said it was her "personal opinion" that British-based B.A.T was the obstacle.

"We were attempting to exercise world leadership," Gregoire said under questioning by Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, who has criticized the proposed settlement in part because it contains no provisions on overseas sales to youths.

Wyden accused the tobacco industry of being willing to sign off on a $368 billion deal that has some protections for young Americans because cigarette makers could make up for the cost by getting "all those kids overseas."

Wyden said he had heard that Gregoire and some other attorneys generals "had worked very hard and very conscientiously to try to get some provision to protect kids overseas... but they (the industry) wouldn't give one inch, not one inch, on their export capabilities overseas."

Mark Smith, a spokesman for Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp, the U.S. division of B.A.T Industries, later told Reuters by telephone, "Brown and Williamson expressed the view that this negotiation should be limited to the United States. It's difficult enough to deal with the domestic issues."
"This view was shared by the other companies," Smith added.
